The effect of rare system-wide resonances in the many-body localization (MBL) transition has recently attracted significant attention. They are expected to play a prominent role in the stability of the MBL phase, prompting the development of new theoretical frameworks to properly account for their s…


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 014210] Published Fri Jul 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies large deviations in the many-body localization transition of the random-field XXZ chain, focusing on rare resonances.
motivation: Rare system-wide resonances are expected to play a prominent role in the stability of the MBL phase, prompting new theoretical frameworks.
method: The authors analyze the random-field XXZ chain, likely using numerical or analytical methods to study large deviations and rare events.
result: The paper provides insights into the effect of rare resonances on the MBL transition, potentially revealing new scaling or universality.
conclusion: The findings contribute to understanding the stability of MBL and the role of rare events, but the connection to information thermodynamics is indirect.

title: Limitations Of Singular Value Decomposition Based Diagnostics For non-Hermitian Many-body Localization With Time-reversal Symmetry
authors: Huimin You, Jinghu Liu, Yunbo Zhang, And Zhihao Xu
abstract:
Author(s): Huimin You, Jinghu Liu, Yunbo Zhang, and Zhihao Xu

Singular value decomposition (SVD) provides a convenient way to construct Hermitian-like diagnostics for non-Hermitian many-body systems, but its reliability for locating many-body localization (MBL) transitions remains unclear, particularly in systems preserving time-reversal symmetry (TRS). We ben…


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 024211] Published Wed Jul 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper investigates the reliability of singular value decomposition (SVD) based diagnostics for detecting many-body localization (MBL) transitions in non-Hermitian systems with time-reversal symmetry.
motivation: SVD provides a convenient Hermitian-like diagnostic for non-Hermitian many-body systems, but its reliability for locating MBL transitions is unclear, especially when time-reversal symmetry is present.
method: The authors benchmark SVD-based diagnostics against known MBL transitions in non-Hermitian systems with time-reversal symmetry, likely using numerical simulations of many-body models.
result: The study reveals limitations of SVD-based diagnostics in accurately identifying MBL transitions under time-reversal symmetry, suggesting they may be unreliable in such contexts.
conclusion: SVD-based diagnostics should be used with caution for non-Hermitian MBL systems with time-reversal symmetry, and alternative methods may be needed.

title: Subordination-based Neural Network Approach For non-Markovian Fokker-Planck Equations
authors: Gege Wang, Wei Wang, Xiaolong Wang, Ralf Metzler, And Yong Xu
abstract:
Author(s): Gege Wang, Wei Wang, Xiaolong Wang, Ralf Metzler, and Yong Xu

The non-Markovian Fokker-Planck equation (FPE) provides an effective description of anomalous diffusion within the classical continuous time random walk framework. However, its nonlocal memory kernel leads to strong non-Markovian behaviors, making the non-Markovian FPE difficult to solve. Convention…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014153] Published Fri Jul 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a neural network approach to solve non-Markovian Fokker-Planck equations describing anomalous diffusion.
motivation: Non-Markovian Fokker-Planck equations are difficult to solve due to memory kernels, limiting their application in modeling anomalous diffusion.
method: The authors develop a subordination-based neural network that transforms the non-Markovian equation into a Markovian one in a subordinated time frame, then uses a neural network to solve the resulting equation.
result: The method accurately solves several non-Markovian FPEs with different memory kernels, demonstrating efficiency and accuracy compared to traditional numerical methods.
conclusion: The subordination-based neural network provides a powerful tool for solving non-Markovian FPEs, facilitating the study of anomalous diffusion in complex systems.

title: Fractional Diffusion Without Disorder In Two Dimensions
authors: Nilotpal Chakraborty, Markus Heyl, And Roderich Moessner
abstract:
Author(s): Nilotpal Chakraborty, Markus Heyl, and Roderich Moessner

We analyze how simple local constraints in two dimensions lead a defect to exhibit robust, nontransient, and tunable subdiffusion. We uncover a rich dynamical phenomenology realized in ice- and dimer-type models. On the microscopic scale, a single defect exhibits anomalously long retractions. Such r…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033118] Published Tue Jul 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies subdiffusion of a defect in two-dimensional ice- and dimer-type models with local constraints, revealing robust and tunable anomalous transport.
motivation: Understanding how local constraints lead to anomalous diffusion in low-dimensional systems is of fundamental interest in statistical mechanics and may have implications for quantum information processing.
method: The authors analyze simple local constraints in two dimensions and study the dynamics of a single defect using analytical and numerical methods.
result: They uncover a rich dynamical phenomenology, including anomalously long retractions and robust, nontransient, tunable subdiffusion.
conclusion: The findings demonstrate that local constraints alone can produce robust subdiffusion without disorder, offering a new mechanism for controlling transport.

title: Hilbert Space Fragmentation In A Driven-dephasing Rydberg Atom Array
authors: Tianyi Yan, Chun Hei Leung, And Weibin Li
abstract:
Author(s): Tianyi Yan, Chun Hei Leung, and Weibin Li

In the driven-dephasing dynamics of a resonant laser-driven chain of strongly interacting Rydberg atoms, multiple long-lived metastable plateaus arise from Hilbert space fragmentation captured by an effective dephasing PXP model. The model supports degenerate zero modes that form disconnected subspaces classified by a consecutive double excitation addressing operator, with the number of subspaces growing exponentially with chain length according to a modified Fibonacci recurrence.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L032015] Published Tue Jul 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies Hilbert space fragmentation in a driven-dephasing Rydberg atom array, leading to long-lived metastable plateaus and an effective dephasing PXP model with degenerate zero modes.
motivation: Understanding the emergence of long-lived metastable states in driven dissipative quantum systems, which is relevant to quantum thermodynamics and non-equilibrium dynamics.
method: The authors model a resonant laser-driven chain of strongly interacting Rydberg atoms with dephasing, deriving an effective dephasing PXP model and analyzing its Hilbert space fragmentation via a consecutive double excitation addressing operator.
result: They find multiple long-lived metastable plateaus arising from Hilbert space fragmentation, with the number of disconnected subspaces growing exponentially according to a modified Fibonacci recurrence.
conclusion: The work reveals a mechanism for metastability in open quantum systems, which may have implications for controlling quantum dynamics and understanding thermalization.

motivation: Understanding how frustration and disorder shape relaxation in complex systems is central to statistical physics and quantum annealing, with implications for optimization and quantum computing.
method: The authors develop a bond-correlated percolation model to analyze spin glass dynamics on complex hardware topologies, likely using numerical simulations and theoretical analysis.
result: The approach provides insights into how frustration and disorder affect relaxation times and the onset of glassy behavior in these systems.

title: Asymptotically Exact Solution Of The non-Hermitian Disordered Interacting Hatano-Nelson Chain
authors: Valéria M. Mattiello, Victor L. Quito, And Eduardo Miranda
abstract:
Author(s): Valéria M. Mattiello, Victor L. Quito, and Eduardo Miranda

This article presents an exact low-energy solution of a one-dimensional model of interacting disordered spinless fermions with non-Hermitian hopping, equivalently formulated as a non-Hermitian spin-1/2 chain. The solution exhibits finite-temperature divergent spin susceptibilities and shows that non-Hermiticity suppresses the entanglement entropy relative to the corresponding Hermitian model, eliminating the associated entanglement scaling.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L032012] Published Wed Jul 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper provides an exact low-energy solution for a non-Hermitian disordered interacting Hatano-Nelson chain, showing that non-Hermiticity suppresses entanglement entropy and eliminates its scaling.
motivation: To understand the interplay between non-Hermiticity, disorder, and interactions in a one-dimensional fermionic system, particularly its thermodynamic and entanglement properties.
method: The authors solve the model exactly using a mapping to a non-Hermitian spin-1/2 chain and analyze its low-energy properties, including spin susceptibilities and entanglement entropy.

Despite recent extensive studies, exact QMBS are rare in dimensions higher than one. This Colloquium discusses the scientific and semantic issues underlying this ambiguity, as well as the history of the field, and offers a definition of active matter as a well-defined subset of nonequilibrium systems. It then surveys recent developments including nonreciprocal interactions, intracellular phase separation, and quantum active matter.

authors: Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, And Guillaume Schull
abstract:
Author(s): Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, and Guillaume Schull

Scanning probe techniques have transformed our ability to study materials at the atomic scale, providing atom-by-atom views of surfaces. Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy combines scanning probes with optical fluorescence. Such optical techniques normally have spatial resolution limited by the wavelength of the light used. However, using the scanning tip itself as a nanoscale optical antenna confines the electromagnetic field to the tip apex, achieving superresolution down to the atomic scale. Fluorescence is a fundamental probe of materials that reveals electronic structure and vibronic properties by exciting electrons to higher levels and observing the photons emitted when they relax. These capabilities are of particular interest for studying and identifying molecules, submolecular structures, and their reactions. This review discusses the techniques of tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy and the new insights they have revealed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025007] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.

motivation: To provide an overview of a scanning probe technique that combines optical fluorescence with atomic-scale resolution, which is important for studying molecular structures.
method: The paper is a review article summarizing the principles and recent advances in tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy.
result: It discusses how the scanning tip acts as an optical antenna to confine electromagnetic fields, enabling superresolution imaging down to the atomic scale.
conclusion: The technique offers new insights into molecular identification and submolecular structures, but it is not directly related to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This review paper discusses the fundamental mechanisms of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on surface defects, electrical stress, and plasma formation.
motivation: Understanding vacuum breakdown is crucial for improving the reliability and efficiency of particle accelerators and other high-power technologies.
method: The paper synthesizes recent experimental and simulation studies to present a coherent mechanistic picture of breakdown initiation and evolution.
result: It identifies key factors such as surface defects, electric field enhancement, and thermal effects that trigger breakdown, and highlights advances in predictive modeling.
conclusion: Improved understanding of vacuum breakdown can lead to better design and operation of high-gradient accelerators and other high-voltage vacuum systems.

title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications, including magnetism, topology, and dynamics.
motivation: To summarize the rapidly evolving field of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials, which has revealed new phenomena and challenged theories.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes current knowledge on 2D magnets, discussing experimental and theoretical advances across various subfields.
result: The review highlights the breadth of the field, including ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, topology, quantum dynamics, and applications in spintronics and magnonics.
conclusion: The field is actively expanding, with potential for new applications, but the paper does not focus on quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on exotic electronic states arising from geometric frustration and interference effects.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind the wealth of exotic phenomena observed in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and orbital antiferromagnetism.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, discussing the role of topology, correlations, and spin-orbit coupling.
result: It highlights the emergence of topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, and various correlated and topological phases in kagome metals.
conclusion: Kagome metals provide a rich platform for exploring novel quantum states, but the paper does not directly contribute to the user's specified research directions.

These systems can be modeled as stochastic reaction-diffusion systems. In this pedagogical review, the authors apply powerful field-theoretic methods to these systems, unifying diverse approaches under a single framework. The methods are useful for handling chemical systems but also have applications in a wide range of areas such as ecology and epidemiology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015001] Published Thu Jan 22, 2026.
tldr: A pedagogical review applying field-theoretic methods to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems, unifying approaches for chemical, ecological, and epidemiological modeling.
motivation: To provide a unified framework for analyzing complex systems modeled as stochastic reaction-diffusion systems, which are prevalent in biology, sociology, and traffic flow.
method: The review synthesizes field-theoretic techniques, including path integrals and quantum methods, to treat stochastic reaction-diffusion systems.
result: It demonstrates how diverse models can be unified under a single field-theoretic framework, offering a comprehensive pedagogical resource.
conclusion: The paper is a valuable educational review but does not directly contribute to the specified research directions in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: This review summarizes how gravitational-wave and X-ray observations of neutron stars constrain the dense matter equation of state.
motivation: Neutron stars are the densest objects in the universe, and their properties provide crucial information about the behavior of matter under extreme compression, which is not directly accessible in terrestrial experiments.
method: The paper reviews recent observational results from gravitational-wave signals of binary neutron star mergers and X-ray pulse profile measurements, and compares them to theoretical predictions from nuclear equation of state calculations extrapolated to high densities.
result: The measurements constrain neutron star masses, radii, and central densities, and the comparisons with theoretical predictions provide insights into the equation of state at supranuclear densities.
conclusion: The review highlights the current state of knowledge and outlines future observational opportunities to further constrain the dense matter equation of state.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation, with emphasis on their synergy.
motivation: To provide an updated overview of spin-glass research, highlighting progress and future opportunities.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes experimental, theoretical, and simulation results in spin-glass dynamics.
result: Summarizes the current state of the field and the importance of interdisciplinary approaches.
conclusion: Spin-glass research benefits from combined experimental, theoretical, and computational efforts, with open questions remaining.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on candidate materials and topological properties.
motivation: Quantum spin liquids are exotic states of matter with potential applications in quantum computing, and Kitaev models provide a solvable framework.
method: The paper reviews theoretical models and experimental progress on Kitaev spin liquids, highlighting candidate materials and their properties.
result: It summarizes the current understanding of Kitaev spin liquids, including chiral edge modes and material candidates.
conclusion: The review provides insights for both experimentalists and theorists, but does not present new results directly relevant to the user's research interests.

title: Statistical Mechanics For Networks Of Real Neurons
authors: Leenoy Meshulam And William Bialek
abstract:
Author(s): Leenoy Meshulam and William Bialek

Our ability to perceive, think, or act relies on coordinated activity in large networks of neurons in the brain. This review examines recent progress in connecting ideas from statistical physics, such as maximum entropy methods and the renormalization group, to quantitative experiments that record the electrical activity of thousands of neurons simultaneously. This quantitative bridge between the new data and statistical physics models uncovers new, quantitatively reproducible behaviors and makes clear that abstract theoretical principles in studies of the brain can have the level of predictive power that we expect in other areas of physics.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045002] Published Thu Nov 06, 2025.
tldr: This review connects statistical physics methods like maximum entropy and renormalization group to large-scale neural recordings, aiming to uncover reproducible collective behaviors in brain networks.
motivation: The authors aim to bridge theoretical statistical physics with experimental neuroscience to find quantitative principles governing neural network activity.
method: The paper reviews recent work applying maximum entropy models and renormalization group techniques to multi-neuron recording data.
result: It highlights that these methods reveal reproducible collective behaviors and predictive power in neural data.
conclusion: Statistical physics provides a powerful framework for understanding complex neural networks, with potential for further theoretical development.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, focusing on photophysical processes relevant to photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: To provide an overview of theoretical approaches for describing internal conversion, a nonradiative process important for applications like photonics and energy harvesting.
method: The paper reviews various theoretical models and methods used to describe internal conversion in quantum systems.
result: The review summarizes the state of the art and outlines how these methods can be applied to relevant applications.
conclusion: The authors present an outlook on incorporating these theoretical methods into studies for photonics and energy harvesting.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews quantum aspects of magnetic skyrmions, focusing on their formation and quantum features, but does not directly address the user's research directions.
motivation: The paper aims to discuss quantum-mechanical properties of magnetic skyrmions, which are topological spin textures with potential applications in spintronics and quantum technologies.
method: It is a review article that synthesizes theoretical and experimental results on skyrmion physics, including interactions and quantum effects.
result: The paper provides an overview of quantum properties of skyrmions, such as their topological nature and possible quantum behavior, but does not present new research findings.
conclusion: The review highlights the current understanding and open questions in quantum skyrmion physics, but it is not aligned with the user's specific interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: This review covers atomic-scale microscopy techniques for measuring disorder in semiconductors, which is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The paper aims to review real-space techniques for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors, which is important for material properties but not directly connected to the user's research interests.
method: The review discusses three real-space techniques: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, and their combined use for characterizing defects.
result: The paper provides an overview of how these techniques can be applied to compound semiconductors to measure disorder.
conclusion: The paper concludes that combining these techniques can provide a more complete picture of defects, but it does not contribute to the user's focus areas.

title: Spin-dependent Exotic Interactions
authors: Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, And Dmitry Budker
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and Dmitry Budker

This review presents a comprehensive summary of theoretical investigations and experimental searches for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model. These interactions may be mediated by various types of exotic bosons, and their existence and properties may, in turn, explain the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The described experiments also probe the discrete fundamental symmetries of nature.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025005] Published Tue Jun 24, 2025.
tldr: This review summarizes theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the standard model, potentially mediated by exotic bosons and related to dark matter and dark energy.
motivation: The paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of spin-dependent exotic interactions, which are motivated by the search for new physics beyond the standard model and the nature of dark matter and dark energy.
method: The review synthesizes theoretical frameworks and experimental techniques used to probe spin-dependent interactions, including precision measurements and searches for symmetry violations.
result: The review catalogs various proposed exotic boson mediators and experimental constraints, highlighting the current status and future prospects in this field.
conclusion: The field of spin-dependent exotic interactions is active and may reveal new physics, but it is not directly aligned with the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:
Author(s): M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. deBoer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, and A. Tumino

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: This review covers the quantum mechanics of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, focusing on tunneling, resonances, and interference effects.
motivation: Stellar nuclear reactions are difficult to measure directly, and theoretical understanding is needed to model stellar burning and element formation.
method: The paper reviews theoretical approaches to low-energy nuclear reactions, including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference, and discusses new experimental ideas.
result: It summarizes the state of the art in theoretical nuclear astrophysics and proposes novel methods to study these reactions in the lab.
conclusion: The review highlights the importance of quantum phenomena in stellar nucleosynthesis and suggests future directions for research.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining that apparent violations arise from violating assumptions in the bounds' derivations.
motivation: To clarify why some measured material properties exceed classical thermodynamic bounds and to show how such violations can be exploited to design novel materials.
method: A review of various physical properties and circumstances where measurements exceed classical thermodynamic bounds, analyzing which underlying assumptions are violated.
result: Identifies multiple cases where apparent violations occur and explains the assumptions violated, also discussing how to design materials that intentionally violate these assumptions.
conclusion: Apparent violations of thermodynamic bounds are due to assumption violations, and understanding this can lead to materials with interesting properties.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews experimental and theoretical approaches to simulating quantum many-body physics in nonstandard geometries such as fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions.
motivation: To explore exotic geometries that enable simulation of phenomena from condensed matter topology to gravity and cosmology, potentially revealing new physics.
method: The paper surveys implementations in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems, discussing theoretical frameworks and experimental techniques for realizing these geometries.
result: It provides a comprehensive overview of current capabilities and challenges in simulating quantum matter in nonstandard geometries, highlighting key achievements and open questions.
conclusion: The field is rapidly advancing, with potential for simulating fundamental physics, but it is not directly aligned with the user's specific research directions in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: This review paper discusses self-alignment in active matter systems, a topic in soft matter physics with no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The paper aims to unify the concept of self-alignment in active matter, which is a key mechanism in biological and robotic systems, but it is outside the user's research interests.
method: The authors provide a review of existing models and experiments, and propose a unified mathematical framework for self-alignment.
result: The review highlights the diverse behaviors arising from self-alignment, such as orbiting and synchronized motion, and its applications in smart materials and robotics.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a powerful principle in active matter, but it does not align with the user's focus on quantum information and related fields.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: This review paper discusses experimental and theoretical efforts to probe gravity using massive quantum systems, focusing on decoherence and entanglement mediated by gravity.
motivation: The authors aim to review the state-of-the-art in testing gravity's quantum effects, as classical gravity is poorly understood and quantum probes may reveal new physics.
method: The paper is a review, summarizing theoretical models and experimental proposals for observing gravitational effects on quantum superpositions and entanglement.
result: It highlights ongoing experiments and theoretical frameworks, but does not present new results.
conclusion: The field is rapidly advancing, and future experiments may determine whether gravity induces decoherence or entanglement, guiding quantum gravity theories.

title: Structural Signatures Of Memory In Amorphous Solids
authors: Dor Shohat And Yoav Lahini Ori Engel
abstract: Amorphous materials can retain memories of past deformations, offering a pathway to understanding their complex energy landscape and self-organization dynamics. These memories are stored in the physical structure; however, reading them from a static structural snapshot remains a challenge and current memory readout protocols rely on dynamic, memory erasing measurements. Here we study several coarse-grained models of amorphous solids with increasing complexity, and demonstrate that the memory of a deformation amplitude can be retrieved from a single structural order parameter. We start from an abstract collection of non-interacting bi-stable elements, where the relation between memory and structural configuration is derived analytically. Using theoretical arguments and numerical simulations, we extend this framework to interacting systems, including one-dimensional chains and two-dimensional networks of coupled bi-stable elements. In the latter case, the order parameter depends on the geometry of the memorized drive. These results point to a general and minimal framework for non-destructive memory retrieval in amorphous materials, from a static snapshot of their internal structure or stress distribution.
tldr: This paper studies memory in amorphous solids using coarse-grained models, showing that deformation amplitude can be retrieved from a static structural order parameter.
motivation: To understand memory storage in amorphous materials and enable non-destructive readout from static snapshots, which is currently challenging.
method: The authors analyze coarse-grained models of amorphous solids, starting with non-interacting bi-stable elements and extending to interacting systems (1D chains and 2D networks), using analytical and numerical approaches.
result: They demonstrate that a single structural order parameter can retrieve the memory of deformation amplitude, with the order parameter depending on geometry in 2D.
conclusion: The work provides a minimal framework for non-destructive memory retrieval in amorphous solids, potentially applicable to materials science.

title: Memory Of Topologically Constrained Disorder In Shakti Artificial Spin Ice
authors: Cristiano Nisoli And Yair Shokef Priyanka Priyanka
abstract: Complex behaviors often sit at a critical threshold between order and disorder. But not all disorder is created equal. Disorder can be trivial or constrained, and correlated disorder can even be topological. Crucially, constrained disorder can harbor memory, leading to non-trivial, sequence-dependent responses to external manipulations. And yet the fascinating subject of ‘memory of disorder’ remains poorly explored, as memory is often associated to the retention of metastable order. In recent years artificial frustrated materials—in particular arrays of frustrated nanomagnets known as artificial spin ices—have been employed to study complex disorders and its wealth of exotic behaviors, yet their memory properties have received much less attention. Here, we investigate both analytically and numerically the sequence-dependent responses of two somehow opposite yet related artificial spin ices: the Landau-ordered square spin ice and the disordered but topologically-ordered Shakti spin ice. We find that Shakti exhibits a pronounced sequence-dependent response, whereas in the square lattice, such path dependence is absent. Within Shakti, even the minimal periodic supercell demonstrates both deterministic and stochastic forms of sequence memory, depending on the interaction strength. Extending our study to cyclic driving, we find that retracing the same input path leads to enhanced memory retention. These results open new perspectives on how topological constraints and correlated disorder generate robust memory effects in frustrated artificial materials, hitherto examined mainly in terms of their ground-state kinetics and thermodynamics.
tldr: This paper studies memory effects in artificial spin ices, focusing on topological constraints and disorder, but does not align with the specified research directions.
motivation: The authors aim to explore how topological constraints and correlated disorder generate robust memory effects in frustrated artificial materials, which have been mainly studied for ground-state kinetics and thermodynamics.
method: They analytically and numerically investigate sequence-dependent responses in two artificial spin ices: Landau-ordered square spin ice and disordered but topologically-ordered Shakti spin ice, including cyclic driving.
result: Shakti exhibits pronounced sequence-dependent response, while square lattice shows no path dependence. Even minimal periodic supercells show deterministic and stochastic memory depending on interaction strength, and cyclic driving enhances memory retention.
conclusion: The findings open new perspectives on memory effects in frustrated artificial materials, but the topic is not within the user's core research areas.

title: Topological Evolution Of Band Degeneracies And Bound States In The Continuum In Anisotropic Photonic Crystal Slabs
authors: Xin Gao, Ze-Huan Zheng, Qilin Duan, Huanyang Chen And Ying Chen
abstract: Topological degeneracies, such as Dirac or Weyl points and exceptional points, play a vital role in photonics and metamaterials due to their unique topological characteristics. This study investigates the intricate evolution of topological charges in degenerate bands, focusing on the interactions among bound states in the continuum (BICs), degenerate states (DS) and circularly polarized states (C points). Specifically, by controlling the optical axis (OA) orientation in anisotropic materials to break azimuthal anisotropy symmetry, we elucidate the evolutionary laws of DS and BICs in momentum space with the rotation of OA, and clarify the accompanying phenomena of charge annihilation and generation. When polar anisotropy symmetry is broken, the complex processes including splitting of BICs, migration of C points and the charge reversal of Γ-point BICs are further displayed. Our work introduces an additional degree of freedom for modulating band degeneracies and their associated topological properties, inspiring future developments in singularity physics through engineering naturally anisotropic materials.
tldr: This paper studies topological charges and bound states in the continuum in anisotropic photonic crystal slabs, focusing on their evolution with optical axis orientation.
motivation: The authors aim to understand and control topological degeneracies (Dirac/Weyl points, exceptional points) in photonic systems, which are important for photonics and metamaterials.
method: They theoretically analyze anisotropic photonic crystal slabs, varying the optical axis orientation to break symmetries and track the evolution of bound states in the continuum (BICs), degenerate states, and circularly polarized states in momentum space.
result: They reveal evolutionary laws for DS and BICs under azimuthal anisotropy breaking, including charge annihilation and generation, and show splitting of BICs, migration of C points, and charge reversal of Γ-point BICs under polar anisotropy breaking.
conclusion: The work introduces a new degree of freedom for modulating band degeneracies and topological properties, potentially inspiring future developments in singularity physics using naturally anisotropic materials.

title: Visualizing The Effect Of Engineered Internal Perturbations On An Artificial 2d Atom And Explaining It Using Perturbation Theory
authors: Marco Weiss And Franz J Giessibl Fabian Stilp
abstract: Atomic orbitals are affected by external perturbations, such as the proximity of other atoms or exposure to electric or magnetic fields, that induce Stark and Zeemann splittings. The thought experiment: What would happen with these orbitals if one would position a fraction of a positive elementary charge with a tweezer at about half the atomic radius? This would allow for a highly controlled experiment on the alteration of atomic orbitals by a perturbation. Such a tweezer does not exist, so this remains a thought experiment. However, we can achieve something similar in an artificial 2D atom such as a quantum corral where we put single adsorbate atoms inside, which can be engineered by lateral manipulation with scanning probe microscopy. We show that the perturbation potential qualitatively follows the one between two natural atoms, a long-range attraction followed by a short-range repulsion. We demonstrate the state-selectivity of the short-range interaction leading to tunable electronic states. Surprisingly, long-range Coulomb attraction can be detected experimentally, even though charges are strongly screened on the metal surface. We estimate an effective charge of the adsorbate on the order of 1/1000 of an elementary charge. The perturbed orbital is imaged by atomic force microscopy and scanning tunneling microscopy and described by perturbation theory. As a practical application, this introduces the ability to tune the geometry of the reactivity of an artificial atom, similar to the change in the chemical reactivity of a natural atom, when it is bound to other atoms.
tldr: This paper uses scanning probe microscopy to visualize and explain the effect of engineered internal perturbations on an artificial 2D atom (quantum corral) via perturbation theory.
motivation: The authors aim to understand how atomic orbitals respond to controlled perturbations, using a quantum corral as a model system to mimic the effect of a nearby charge.
method: They engineered perturbations by placing adsorbate atoms inside a quantum corral using lateral manipulation, then imaged the resulting electronic states with AFM and STM, and compared with perturbation theory.
result: They observed state-selective short-range interactions and long-range Coulomb attraction despite screening, estimating an effective charge of ~1/1000 of an elementary charge.
conclusion: The work demonstrates the ability to tune the electronic structure and reactivity of an artificial atom, with potential applications in controlling chemical reactivity at the nanoscale.

title: Probing Quark Electromagnetic Properties Via Entangled Quark Pairs In Fragmentation Hadrons At Lepton Colliders
authors: Qing-Hong Cao, Guanghui Li, Xin-Kai Wen And Bin Yan
abstract: Electromagnetic dipole interactions of light quarks induce distinct spin correlations in quark pairs produced at lepton colliders, favoring entangled spin-triplet state aligned along the axis or spin-singlet state. These correlations lead to unique azimuthal asymmetries in inclusive -dihadron pair production and in back-to-back hadron pairs ( ), which are absent in the SM. Using published Belle and BaBar measurements together with projected sensitivities based on ratios of azimuthal asymmetries, we demonstrate that these measurements provide significant constraints on light-quark dipole couplings, with a reduced dependence on poorly known nonperturbative fragmentation functions and free from contamination by other new physics effects. This approach offers a clean and novel probe of light-quark dipole interactions in collider experiments.
tldr: This paper proposes using spin correlations in entangled quark pairs from lepton colliders to probe light-quark electromagnetic dipole moments, but it is a high-energy phenomenology study unrelated to the specified research directions.
motivation: The authors aim to find a clean probe of light-quark dipole interactions, which are poorly constrained and could indicate new physics.
method: They analyze spin correlations in quark-antiquark pairs produced at lepton colliders, focusing on azimuthal asymmetries in dihadron production, and use Belle/BaBar data plus projected sensitivities.
result: They show that these asymmetries can significantly constrain light-quark dipole couplings with reduced dependence on fragmentation functions.
conclusion: This provides a novel collider probe of quark dipole moments, but it is not aligned with the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: El Agente Cuántico: Automating Quantum Simulations
authors: Ignacio Gustin, Luis Mantilla Calderón, Juan B Pérez-Sánchez, Chris Crebolder, Jérôme F Gonthier, Mohammad Ghazi Vakili, Yuma Nakamura, Karthik Panicker, Manav Ramprasad, Aiwei Yin, Zijian Zhang, Yunheng Zou, Varinia Bernales And Alán Aspuru-Guzik
abstract: Quantum simulation is central to understanding and designing quantum systems across physics and chemistry. However, its practical use is often limited by the exponential growth of Hilbert space and by the increasing complexity of modern quantum-simulation software. Here we introduce El Agente Cuántico, a multi-agent AI system that automates quantum-simulation workflows by translating natural-language scientific intent into executed and validated computations across heterogeneous quantum-software frameworks. By reasoning directly over library documentation and APIs, our agentic system dynamically assembles end-to-end simulations spanning—but not limited to—state preparation, closed- and open-system dynamics, tensor-network methods, quantum control, quantum error correction, and quantum resource estimation. The developed system unifies traditionally distinct simulation paradigms behind a single natural-language interface. Beyond reducing technical barriers, this approach opens a path toward scalable, adaptive, and increasingly autonomous quantum simulation, enabling faster exploration of physical models, rapid hypothesis testing, and closer integration between theory, simulation, and emerging quantum hardware.
tldr: This paper introduces an AI agent system for automating quantum simulations via natural language, but it does not align with the specified research directions.
motivation: Quantum simulation is limited by complexity and software heterogeneity; the authors aim to lower barriers and automate workflows.
method: They develop a multi-agent AI system that interprets natural language, reasons over documentation/APIs, and assembles simulations across various quantum software frameworks.

title: From Intuition To Optimization: A Review Of Inverse Design Applied To Optical Nanotweezers
authors: Sejeong Kim And Kenneth B Crozier Damian Nelson
abstract: Optical nanotweezers, which integrate nanophotonic structures such as plasmonic antennas, dielectric resonators, and metasurfaces, have emerged as powerful tools for manipulating nanoparticles, biomolecules, and viruses with high precision. However, traditional designs rely heavily on heuristic approaches and simple geometries, limiting performance. Inverse design offers a paradigm shift by using computational optimization methods to discover non-intuitive, high-performance structures for optical trapping. This review provides an overview of key inverse design methodologies, including adjoint-based optimization, topology optimization, and machine learning approaches, and highlights their broader impact across nanophotonics. We then focus on their application to optical nanotweezers, where recent advances demonstrate enhanced trapping stiffness, reduced optical heating, and tailored trapping landscapes. Representative examples include algorithmic design of plasmonic nanotweezers, topology-optimized plasmonic nanoapertures, inverse-designed dielectric nanocavities, and force-centric designs based on Maxwell stress tensor engineering. Collectively, these studies illustrate how inverse design enables stable, efficient, and versatile optical trapping at the nanoscale. Despite these advances, challenges remain in fabrication, computational cost, and the interpretability of optimized structures. We conclude with a perspective on future directions, emphasizing opportunities in reconfigurable tweezers, lab-on-a-chip integration, and quantum nanophotonics. By bridging photonic optimization with nanoscale manipulation, inverse-designed optical nanotweezers offer promising opportunities for future applications in biophysics, materials science, and quantum technologies.
tldr: A review of inverse design methods applied to optical nanotweezers, focusing on computational optimization for nanophotonic trapping structures.
motivation: Traditional optical tweezers rely on heuristic designs with limited performance; inverse design offers a computational approach to discover high-performance structures.
method: The paper reviews adjoint-based optimization, topology optimization, and machine learning approaches, and discusses their application to optical nanotweezers.
result: Inverse design enhances trapping stiffness, reduces heating, and enables tailored trapping landscapes, with examples including plasmonic and dielectric designs.
conclusion: Inverse-designed optical nanotweezers show promise for biophysics, materials science, and quantum technologies, but face challenges in fabrication, cost, and interpretability.

title: Review On Band Structure And Spin Polarization Of Altermagnetic Materials
authors: Xiangnan Xie, Xiaoyue He, Fayuan Zhang And Chaoyu Chen
abstract: Recent theoretical and experimental efforts have revealed the existence of a new class of magnetic materials, altermagnets, characterized by distinct symmetries in spin and real space. Combining the properties of ferromagnets, such as band spin polarization and time-reversal symmetry breaking responses, and antiferromagnets, like vanishing stray field and terahertz magnon dynamics, altermagnets are attracting enormous attention in both magnetism and spintronics community. While numerous altermagnetic candidates and emerging physical properties have been studied in theory extensively and enthusiastically, the experimental investigation of altermagnetism is struggling against the lack of proper altermagnetic materials and the controversial results reported for specific candidates. In this review, we first give a general description on the concept and key properties of altermagnetism, outline its distinction from other compensated magnetic order from the aspects of time-reversal symmetry in the spin momentum locking texture and time-reversal symmetry breaking responses. The main body of this review concentrates on the progress in altermagnetic material study with special focus on their band structure and spin polarization features, as well as the controversies over several candidate materials. Going forward, we point out several directions which altermagnetic material investigation might follow and guidelines which could help to avoid the pitfalls in the experimental pursuit of ideal altermagnets.
tldr: A review of altermagnetic materials focusing on their band structure and spin polarization, highlighting experimental challenges.
motivation: To consolidate theoretical and experimental progress on altermagnets, a new class of magnetic materials with potential spintronic applications, and to address controversies in candidate materials.
method: The paper reviews the concept of altermagnetism, contrasts it with other magnetic orders, and surveys experimental studies of band structure and spin polarization in candidate materials.
result: Summarizes key properties and experimental findings, identifies controversies, and suggests future research directions and guidelines for avoiding pitfalls.
conclusion: Altermagnets are promising but experimental verification is challenging; more work is needed to identify and characterize ideal materials.

title: Switchable Band Alignment In 2D-perovskite/WS2 Heterostructures For Tunable Exciton Transport And Valley Polarization
authors: Yingying Chen, Zeyi Liu, Zisheng Gong, Cheng Wang, Wendian Yao, Junze Li, Ti Wang, Weibo Gao And Dehui Li
abstract: Van der Waals heterostructures integrated by two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) hold great potential for engineering promising exciton phenomena, particularly interlayer excitons (IXs) featuring extended lifetimes and permanent out-of-plane electric dipole moments. While electrically controllable IX emission has been extensively explored in TMD heterobilayers, reconfiguring their band alignment to achieve selected exciton states and exploit these states for novel excitonic functionalities remains an urgent challenge. Here, we demonstrate dynamic exciton control by electrically tunable band alignment transitions between type-II and type-I configurations in WS2/(iso-BA)2PbI4 heterostructures, enabling reversible conversion between charged interlayer (IX±) and charged intralayer (X−) excitons. By tailoring these exciton states, we achieve two critical functionalities: (i) 7 μm ON/OFF control of exciton transport via transition between delocalized IX± (ON) and confined X− (OFF) states; (ii) valley polarization switching with a 16.3 ON/OFF ratio, leveraging distinct spin-valley configurations of IX± (unpolarized) and X− (polarized). Unlike twist-angle-dependent TMD heterobilayers, this platform operates independently of stacking alignment, establishing a broadly hybrid 2D system as a practical paradigm towards programmable nanophotonic circuits.

motivation: The authors aim to achieve dynamic control of exciton states in van der Waals heterostructures, which is crucial for programmable nanophotonic circuits.
method: They fabricate WS2/(iso-BA)2PbI4 heterostructures and apply electric fields to switch between type-II and type-I band alignments, converting between charged interlayer and intralayer excitons.
result: They achieve 7 μm ON/OFF control of exciton transport and valley polarization switching with a 16.3 ON/OFF ratio.
conclusion: This platform offers a twist-angle-independent approach for tunable exciton functionalities, potentially advancing nanophotonic applications.

title: Exploring Exotic Spin-dependent Interactions Beyond The Standard Model: Theoretical Foundations And Experimental Investigations
authors: L Y Wu And H Yan
abstract: New interactions mediated by novel particles propose solutions to several important questions in modern physics. Axions serve as examples of such particles; they are lightweight and interact weakly with ordinary matter. This category of particles, including those similar to axions—termed axion-like particles (ALPs)—arises from diverse theoretical frameworks, such as the Peccei-Quinn mechanism addressing the strong CP problem, string theory, and spontaneous supersymmetry breaking. Given their light mass and weak coupling, ALPs are also possible candidates for cold dark matter. Introducing these new interactions mediated by novel particles not only tackles several challenges in modern physics but also raises a crucial question: Are there undiscovered interactions beyond the standard model (SM)? Many of the interactions predicted by these theories are spin-dependent, which is the primary focus of this review. In this review, we first outline the theoretical foundations for investigating exotic spin-dependent interactions, highlighting their importance in various models beyond the SM. We examine the potential roles of new lightweight particles in mediating these interactions, which may enhance our understanding of dark matter. Relevant formulas derived from theoretical models are included to support experimental investigations. Following this theoretical framework, we conduct a detailed review of recent experimental efforts to detect these exotic interactions. A systematic review of current constraints on these interactions is presented, along with an assessment of various detection approaches.
tldr: A review of theoretical and experimental efforts to detect exotic spin-dependent interactions mediated by axion-like particles, focusing on physics beyond the Standard Model.
motivation: To explore potential new forces beyond the Standard Model that could address open questions in physics, such as dark matter and the strong CP problem.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks for spin-dependent interactions and summarizes experimental constraints from various detection approaches.
result: It provides a systematic overview of current constraints on these interactions and assesses different detection methods.
conclusion: The review highlights the ongoing search for new physics but does not present novel results directly applicable to the user's research directions.

title: Non-spreading Meronic Spin Defects Around Optical Vortices
authors: Miguel A Porras And Yijie Shen Nilo Mata-Cervera
abstract: Optical vortices are singularity lines where the light field intensity vanishes and its phase is undefined. These threads of darkness are adorned by Gauss’s law as lines of pure longitudinal polarization where the polarization plane tilts and winds around. The resulting spin field is as a unique structure with both features of topological texture and defect, as it includes a point defect of undefined spin enclosed by a meronic texture which spans half the spin unit sphere. This topological structure does not spread in propagation: the normalized spin field maintains a deep-subwavelength confinement around the vortex line while the underlying vortex beam continues to diffract. From their intrinsic nature and subwavelength confinement, these textures exhibit enhanced robustness upon isotropic perturbations such as atmospheric turbulence compared with other tailored polarization textures. Here we describe these topologies of transverse spin which decorate the phase singularity of paraxial vortex beams, highlighting the diversity of topological structures that arise in two different spaces—the spin unit sphere and the transverse-axial Poincaré sphere—and discuss the underlying aspects behind their subwavelength localization.

method: The paper provides a theoretical description of the spin field around optical vortices, analyzing the topology on the spin unit sphere and the transverse-axial Poincaré sphere, and discusses the physical mechanisms behind subwavelength localization.
result: They find that the normalized spin field forms a meronic texture with a point defect, remains confined at deep-subwavelength scales during propagation, and exhibits enhanced robustness to isotropic perturbations like atmospheric turbulence.
conclusion: The work reveals a new class of topological spin textures in optics with potential applications in structured light and optical manipulation, but it does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Self-sustained Electric Field-driven Off-grid Platform For On-demand Microdroplet Charging And Programmable Manipulation
authors: Jeongseok Oh And Dongwhi Choi Donghan Lee
abstract: Power independence and system simplicity are paramount for robust droplet manipulation in decentralized applications, including point-of-care diagnostics and wearable biosensors. However, conventional active microfluidics for droplet manipulation are often bottlenecked by the requirement for high-voltage power supplies, intricate electrode networks, or magnetic additives that escalate system complexity and restrict portability. Here, we report a self-sustained electric-field-based electrophoretic platform (SELF-EP) that achieves autonomous droplet charging and sophisticated manipulation, entirely eliminating the need for external power sources. This is enabled by a specialized SELF emitter engineered to retain quasi-permanent surface charges, providing a continuous and stable SELF. Rather than direct charge injection, SELF drives electrostatic induction, drawing charges from ground to induce a net charge on droplets. Through integrated theoretical modeling and experimental validation, we demonstrate that the SELF-EP allows for deterministic control of droplet charge and supports on-demand droplet manipulation with various spatial configurations. Notably, we show parallelized control of multiple droplets and realize complex, programmable functions such as self-alignment and routing via precise spatial patterning of surface charges. Our SELF-EP paradigm bypasses the need for active electronics, offering a minimalist yet multifunctional strategy that significantly expands the boundaries of autonomous microfluidic and biomedical technologies.
tldr: This paper presents a self-sustained electric-field-based platform for droplet manipulation without external power, which is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The authors aim to overcome limitations of conventional active microfluidics, such as high-voltage power supplies and complex electrode networks, to enable portable and autonomous droplet manipulation for point-of-care diagnostics and wearable biosensors.
method: They design a SELF emitter that retains quasi-permanent surface charges, generating a stable electric field that induces charges on droplets via electrostatic induction, and they combine theoretical modeling with experiments to demonstrate controlled droplet charging and manipulation.
result: The platform achieves deterministic control of droplet charge and enables programmable functions like self-alignment and routing, with parallelized control of multiple droplets.
conclusion: The SELF-EP paradigm offers a minimalist, power-independent strategy for autonomous microfluidics, expanding possibilities in biomedical technologies.

title: Colloquium: Hadron Production In Open-charm Meson Pairs At ${e}^{+}{e}^{−}$ Colliders
authors: Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, And Yuanning Gao
abstract:
Author(s): Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, and Yuanning Gao

Hadron spectroscopy is a frontier of particle physics; searching for new hadrons is crucial for validating the theory of strong interaction (QCD). Investigating how charmonium, a bound state of charm and anticharm quarks, decays and searching for new charmoniumlike states yield valuable insights into strong interaction mechanisms, including quark confinement and gluon binding. Hadrons produced at e− collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs are a primary source of experimental information for these investigations. This Colloquium reviews current progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments. As BESIII accumulates high-precision data, it has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems, and recent advances are highlighted.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021001] Published Fri Apr 03, 2026.

method: It reviews results from experiments such as BaBar, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII, highlighting recent advances in measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems.
result: The review emphasizes BESIII's leading role in high-precision measurements of hadron production in open-charm meson pairs.
conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive overview of current knowledge and recent progress in this area of particle physics.

title: Colloquium: Planetary Radar At The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, And Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín
abstract:
Author(s): Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, and Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín

For more than two decades, the planetary radar installed at the Arecibo Telescope was the most sensitive instrument of its kind, harnessing the penetrating power of radio waves to perform observations of the (sub)surface of planets, moons, and asteroids in the Solar System—providing a unique perspective on those bodies that helped to drive in situ exploration. This Colloquium presents an overview of the scientific legacy of the Arecibo radar system, focusing on the period posterior to the Gregorian Update in the late 1990s until the unexpected demise of the telescope in 2020. After recalling the basics of planetary radar techniques, it reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, our Moon, and the Saturn system, and highlights its essential role in the characterization of a large sample of near-Earth asteroids and comets.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011003] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.

method: It is a review article that summarizes radar techniques and key observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, the Moon, the Saturn system, and near-Earth asteroids and comets.
result: The paper highlights the radar's unique capabilities in probing surfaces and subsurfaces, aiding in situ exploration, and characterizing near-Earth objects.
conclusion: The Arecibo radar was a unique and powerful tool for planetary radar astronomy, and its loss is significant for the field.

title: Colloquium: Radio Astronomy With The Arecibo 305-m Telescope: In Contemporaneous Context
authors: Tapasi Ghosh And Chris Salter
abstract:
Author(s): Tapasi Ghosh and Chris Salter

The Arecibo Observatory, inaugurated in 1963 as the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, remained at the forefront of astronomy and atmospheric science for more than five decades, until its catastrophic collapse in December 2020. This Colloquium focuses on Arecibo’s enduring legacy in radio astronomy, offering a historical perspective that emphasizes how successive major upgrades of the telescope continuously expanded its observational capabilities and scientific impact. It presents Arecibo’s most influential contributions in topics as diverse as pulsar studies, the mapping of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the Milky Way and other galaxies, the characterization of the interstellar medium, the imaging of extragalactic radio sources with very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), and being a major contributor to the first-ever detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.

title: Colloquium: The Cosmic Dipole Anomaly
authors: Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, And Subir Sarkar
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, and Subir Sarkar

The cosmological principle, which states that the Universe must be statistically isotropic and homogeneous on large scales, is a foundational principle of the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). The validity of this principle can be tested by assessing the compatibility of a dipole anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of matter with the dipole observed in the cosmic microwave background, interpreted in the ΛCDM model as due to our local peculiar motion. This Colloquium describes the methodology for such a test and presents its outcome based on the analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, revealing a significant inconsistency between the two dipoles. The authors review these recent findings, as well as potential biases, systematic issues, and alternate interpretations, and discuss how this anomaly could challenge the standard description of our Universe based on the ΛCDM model.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041001] Published Thu Dec 11, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the cosmic dipole anomaly, a cosmological observation that challenges the standard model of cosmology, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The paper addresses a potential inconsistency in the cosmological principle, which is a foundational assumption of the standard model of cosmology. It aims to assess whether the observed dipole in large-scale structure matches the cosmic microwave background dipole.
method: The authors review recent analyses of large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, comparing the dipole anisotropy in their distribution with the CMB dipole. They discuss potential biases, systematic effects, and alternative interpretations.
result: The analyses reveal a significant inconsistency between the cosmic dipole and the CMB dipole, suggesting a possible violation of the cosmological principle.
conclusion: The cosmic dipole anomaly could challenge the standard ΛCDM model, but further investigation is needed to rule out systematic effects and confirm the anomaly.
